# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand encompasses a broad range of provisions from early childhood through tertiary levels. Early childhood education is delivered through both teacher-led and parent-led services, regulated by the Ministry of Education and guided by the Te Whāriki curriculum framework. Primary and secondary education are free for residents and compulsory from ages 6 to 16, though most children begin at age 5. The system is structured as Years 1–13, with primary education through Year 8, and secondary education through Year 13. The national curriculum—The New Zealand Curriculum (NZC) for English-medium and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa for Māori-medium schools—dictates learning in eight core areas with NCEA serving as the principal qualification in the senior years. School types include state, state-integrated, and private schools, each with distinct funding models.
Efforts to revitalize Māori language and education are reflected through Māori-medium schools (Kura Kaupapa Māori, kōhanga reo), and language immersion programs. While historic policies suppressed Māori language in schools, recent decades have seen its restoration and protection under law. School funding varies by decile, with lower-decile schools receiving more support. Tertiary education comprises universities, polytechnics, and other institutions under the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, funded by a mix of government contributions and student fees, with student loans and allowances available. Despite strong participation rates, New Zealand faces ongoing concerns about educational standards, mathematical proficiency, and bullying. Māori and Pacific Island students, in particular, continue to experience achievement disparities compared to Pākehā counterparts, though Māori-focused educational initiatives have shown promising results.
